target_customer: Small and mid-size businesses needing a hosted VPN without buying hardware, plus privacy-minded consumers for the Privacy VPN product
problem: Companies had to buy and run VPN hardware from vendors like Cisco and Juniper to give staff secure remote access. CryptoSeal sold VPN as a cloud service with no on-premise gear.
business_model: Subscription VPN as a service (enterprise Connect plan listed at 99 USD per month for five users) plus a consumer privacy VPN
product_category: VPN as a service, server key management, trusted computing

founders.name: Ryan Lackey
previous_startups: A project to host content at the Sealand fortress with Sean Hastings (left after costs proved high)
founders.background_notes: Cloudflare Q&A says he did cryptographic software for payment systems, RFID/NFC card payments and about six years of defense contracting on wireless networks, without naming employers. Education not found. YC page calls him a cypherpunk.

founders.name: Erik Berls
founders.background_notes: YC page lists him as the technical founder.

founders.name: Thomas Sparks
founders.background_notes: YC page describes an infrastructure professional focused on colocation and network buildouts.

competitors.name: Cisco and Juniper
competitors.what: Sold VPN hardware and gateway equipment to businesses

technical_complexity.rationale: Standard VPN protocols run in the cloud with multi-platform clients, plus key management and trusted computing ambitions. Hard parts were security hygiene and cross-platform clients, not novel research.

defensibility.rationale: Hosted VPN was built from open protocols and was easy to copy; the only differentiator was a security-first reputation.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: CloudFlare acquired the enterprise VPN business in June 2014, retired the service by June 30 and hired the CEO as a product manager.

market_need_then: Businesses were moving to cloud applications and mobile work and wanted VPN access without hardware. After the 2013 Lavabit case, demand for privacy services drew attention, but the same legal risk led CryptoSeal to close its consumer product.

branding.domain_note: Used cryptoseal.com; no acquisition history found.

identity.voice_and_tone: Security-first, principled; the October 2013 shutdown statement framed closing the product as protecting users from forced key disclosure.

branding.brand_signature: The public decision to shut its privacy VPN rather than risk handing over keys
branding.community_and_virality: Shutdown drew coverage from The Register, Techdirt, Boing Boing, Softpedia and The Hacker News in October 2013.

brand_strength.rationale: Little brand identity evidence beyond press coverage of the 2013 shutdown, which gave it security-community recognition.

outcome_analysis: CryptoSeal sold hosted VPNs from 2012 and drew press when it closed its consumer Privacy VPN in October 2013 over fears of government key demands after Lavabit. The enterprise business was bought by CloudFlare in June 2014 with terms undisclosed, and the CEO joined CloudFlare, so the outcome looks like a small acquisition tied to the team and its security expertise.
